chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Board, the Auditor and the Pay Packet

lessons.title: Reading the Board: Independent Directors, Tenure and Real Independence

body.text: A board is independent on paper when it has enough independent directors. It is independent in practice only when those directors are willing, and able, to say no to the promoter.

children.text: In Chapter 2 you saw how a promoter can control a company with a majority stake, or even much less. The board is the one body meant to stand between that control and your money. Independent directors approve related party transactions, set management pay, and oversee the auditor. When they do the job, a controlling promoter still has to justify every deal that affects minority shareholders. When they do not, the board becomes a rubber stamp with impressive names on it, which is exactly what Satyam's shareholders discovered in December 2008.
The Rules: What Every Listed Board Must Have

Board requirements come from two places: the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's LODR Regulations. The LODR rules are stricter and apply to every company listed on NSE and BSE. Know the minimums, because a board that only just meets them tells you something, and a board that fails them tells you more.

body.caption: Key board rules for Indian listed companies

cells: Board independence
At least half the board independent if the chairperson is an executive or related to the promoter; at least one third if the chairperson is a non-executive not related to the promoter
LODR Regulation 17
Tenure
Up to five consecutive years per term, a maximum of two terms, then a three-year cooling-off period before returning to the same company
Companies Act, 2013, Section 149
Appointment
Appointment, reappointment, and removal of independent directors need shareholder approval by special resolution
LODR Regulation 25
Audit committee
At least two thirds independent, chaired by an independent director; only independent directors on the committee vote on related party transactions
LODR Regulations 18 and 23
Nomination and remuneration committee
At least two thirds independent, chaired by an independent director
LODR Regulation 19
Meetings
At least four board meetings a year, with no more than 120 days between two meetings; independent directors meet separately at least once a year
LODR Regulation 17; Schedule IV of the Companies Act
Directorship limits
An independent director can serve on the boards of at most seven listed companies, or three if they are a whole-time director of any listed company
LODR Regulation 17A

stats.label: Maximum tenure
stats.context: Two terms of up to five years each

body.title: Tenure Rule
body.textWithBlank: After serving two consecutive terms, an independent director must wait for a cooling-off period of ___ years before being appointed to the same company again.
body.explanation: Section 149 of the Companies Act, 2013 caps independent directors at two consecutive terms of up to five years each, followed by a three-year cooling-off period. The rule exists because long tenure erodes independence.

children.text: Independent on Paper vs Independent in Practice

The legal test for independence in Section 149(6) is mostly about what a director is not: not a promoter or relative, not a recent employee or key managerial person, not a partner of the audit firm in the last three years, not holding 2% or more of the voting power, and without significant financial dealings with the company. A director can pass every one of these tests and still owe their seat, their prestige, and their annual commission to the promoter who nominated them. Your job is to look past the label.

columns.label: Independent on Paper
points: Meets every legal test in Section 149(6)
Long personal or professional ties to the promoter family
Sits on several boards within the same business group
Close to the 10-year limit, or returned straight after a cooling-off period
Rarely attends, never asks for independent advice, no recorded dissent

columns.label: Independent in Practice
points: Brings relevant expertise the board actually needs, such as audit, sector, or risk
Has a reputation outside this company that they would not risk
Limited other board commitments, so has time to do the work
Attends nearly every board and committee meeting
Visible willingness to challenge, such as questioning deals or resigning with specific reasons

body.caption: Seven practical tests of real independence

cells: Tenure
Directors in their eighth to tenth year, or who were on the board in another capacity before becoming independent
Director profiles in the annual report and AGM notice
Past relationships
Former employees, former CFOs, lawyers or consultants to the promoter family, or retired executives of group companies
Director profiles; related party note for fees paid to firms linked to directors
Group directorships
The same person as an independent director across several companies of one business group
Corporate governance report, list of other directorships
Attendance
Attendance well below 75% of board and committee meetings
Corporate governance report, attendance table
Expertise
An audit committee without anyone with a real finance or audit background
Skills and expertise matrix in the corporate governance report
Pay
Commission to independent directors that is large relative to their other income, creating dependence on the seat
Remuneration details in the corporate governance report
Shareholder votes
A large share of public institutional shareholders voting against the director's appointment or reappointment
Voting results filed on BSE and NSE after the AGM

body.text: The single best document for this work is the Corporate Governance Report inside the annual report. It lists every director's category, other directorships, committee memberships, meetings attended, and the board's skills matrix. Most investors never open it. Twenty minutes with it tells you more about a board than any number of glossy chairman's letters.

children.text: Read the Votes, Not Just the Result

Under LODR Regulation 44, companies must file detailed voting results with the exchanges within two working days of a general meeting, split into promoter and promoter group, public institutions, and public non-institutions. A resolution that passes with 90% support can hide the fact that most independent shareholders voted against it. Proxy advisory firms such as IiAS, InGovern, and SES publish voting recommendations on board appointments, and institutional investors often follow them, so a large institutional 'against' vote is usually a considered one.

Consider an illustrative special resolution to reappoint an independent director for a second term. 80 crore votes are cast. Promoters cast 50 crore votes, all in favour. Public institutions cast 25 crore votes: 7.5 crore for and 17.5 crore against. Public non-institutions cast 5 crore votes: 4 crore for and 1 crore against.

body.title: Votes cast on the reappointment (crore votes)
Did It Pass?
body.prompt: Using the votes above, what percentage of total votes cast were in favour of the reappointment? A special resolution needs at least 75%. Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Votes for = 50 + 7.5 + 4 = 61.5 crore. Total votes cast = 80 crore. 61.5 ÷ 80 = 76.875%, so the special resolution passes. But look at the non-promoter votes: only 11.5 crore of 30 crore, or 38.3%, supported the director, and 70% of institutional votes were against. The director is 'independent' largely because the promoter voted them in, which is exactly the signal the headline result hides.

children.text: When Independence Is Tested: Two Real Episodes
Tata Group, 2016: The Independent Director Who Dissented

events.title: Cyrus Mistry removed as Tata Sons chairman
events.description: The board of Tata Sons, the unlisted holding company and promoter of the listed Tata companies, replaces its chairman.

events.title: Nusli Wadia publicly backs Mistry
events.description: Wadia, an independent director on the boards of listed companies Tata Motors, Tata Steel, and Tata Chemicals, supports Mistry's continuation as chairman of those companies.

events.title: Promoter calls EGMs to remove him
events.description: Tata Sons requisitions extraordinary general meetings, and Wadia is voted off the boards of all three companies, with the promoter's votes deciding the outcome.

children.text: Set aside who was right in the dispute. The governance lesson is structural: an independent director who takes a position the promoter disagrees with can be removed by the promoter's own votes. That is one reason SEBI later moved to require special resolutions for appointing and removing independent directors, which makes it harder, though not impossible, for a large promoter to act alone.
ICICI Bank, 2018: The Board That Backed Too Fast

In March 2018, after allegations of a conflict of interest involving loans to the Videocon group and the business interests of the CEO's husband, ICICI Bank's board publicly expressed full faith and confidence in its CEO, Chanda Kochhar, based on a preliminary internal review. Months later, under pressure, the board commissioned an independent inquiry led by retired Supreme Court judge Justice B.N. Srikrishna. Kochhar resigned in October 2018, and in January 2019 the board, acting on the inquiry's findings that she had violated the bank's code of conduct, treated her exit as a termination for cause. ICICI Bank has no promoter, which makes the point sharper: a board can fail to act independently of a powerful CEO, not just a promoter.

body.text: A board rushing to publicly defend management before any independent investigation is a governance red flag in itself. Good boards say they are investigating, appoint someone outside the company to do it, and reserve judgement until it is done.

body.title: Who Is Least Independent?
body.question: All four people below legally qualify as independent directors of a family-controlled listed company. Who is most likely to be independent only on paper?
options: A chartered accountant with no prior link to the company, on three listed boards, who chairs the audit committee and attended every meeting
A retired banker in the ninth year of their tenure, who is also an independent director on four other companies in the same promoter group
A sector expert appointed last year after a proxy advisor supported the appointment and 85% of institutional votes were in favour
A former SEBI official with no other board seats who has asked for an external valuation of a proposed related party deal
body.explanation: Long tenure near the 10-year limit plus seats across five companies of the same group means this director's professional standing and income are heavily tied to one promoter family. That does not prove they are compromised, but it makes challenging the promoter costly for them. The other three show signs of real independence: relevant expertise, full attendance, strong institutional support, or active scrutiny of related party deals.

body.title: Score This Board
body.scenario: A family-controlled NSE-listed company has six directors. The chairman and managing director is the promoter. His son is an executive director. The four independent directors are: (1) the company's former CFO, who retired four years ago; (2) a senior partner at a law firm that advises the promoter family's private trusts; (3) a retired industrialist in their ninth year on the board, who is also an independent director on five other companies of the same group; (4) a retired civil servant appointed last year, who attended 3 of 6 board meetings. The audit committee is made up of directors (1), (2), and (3), chaired by the former CFO. At the last AGM, 64% of public institutional votes went against reappointing director (3).
body.prompt: Does this board meet the legal requirements? Is it independent in practice? What does it mean for how you read this company's related party transactions?
body.modelAnswer: Legally, it likely passes. With an executive promoter chairman, at least half the board must be independent, and four of six is two thirds. The former CFO passes the three-year gap, and the law firm fees may be below the materiality thresholds. In practice, independence is weak. The former CFO is reviewing accounts built on systems they designed and likely has close ties to management. The lawyer's firm earns fees from the promoter family, so challenging the promoter has a direct cost. Director (3) is effectively a group insider after nine years and five group board seats, and most institutions voted against them. Director (4) is the most independent on paper but attends only half the meetings. The audit committee, which is the body that approves related party transactions, is made up entirely of the three weakest directors. So treat every related party transaction in this company as if no independent review took place, read the related party note line by line, and demand much stronger evidence of arm's length pricing before trusting it.

body.title: What an independent director's resignation letter must now disclose

children.text: When an independent director resigns before their term ends, the company must disclose it to the exchanges along with the detailed reasons given by the director and the director's confirmation that there are no other material reasons beyond those stated. The resignation letter itself is filed. An independent director who resigns also cannot join the same company as a whole-time director within a year. Read these letters in full. Phrases like 'pre-occupation' or 'personal reasons' are common and often genuine, but a letter mentioning lack of information, disagreement with a decision, or concerns about governance is one of the most direct warnings a board can send you. Director and auditor resignations are covered in more depth in the next two lessons and the case study at the end of this chapter.

body.title: Read the Board of One of Your Holdings
steps: Open the latest annual report from the Documents section on screener.in and go to the Corporate Governance Report
List every director with their category: promoter, executive, non-executive, or independent. Check that at least half are independent if the chairperson is an executive or promoter
For each independent director, note tenure, other directorships, and whether any are in the same business group
Check attendance for board and audit committee meetings, and flag anyone below 75%
Read each independent director's profile in the AGM notice for past links to the company, its auditors, or the promoter family
Open the last AGM voting results on BSE or NSE and find the public institutional vote on any director appointment or reappointment
Search exchange announcements for independent director resignations in the last three years and read the stated reasons

body.text: Companies and individuals named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures and widely reported events, for education only. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security, or a judgement on any party to those disputes.

points: Independent directors approve related party transactions, set pay, and oversee the auditor, making them minority shareholders' main protection inside the company
LODR requires at least half the board to be independent when the chairperson is an executive or promoter, with independent-majority audit and nomination committees
Independent directors serve at most two five-year terms, cannot take ESOPs, and sitting fees are capped at ₹1 lakh per meeting
Legal independence is not practical independence: check tenure, past relationships, group directorships, attendance, expertise, and pay
Read voting results by category; a resolution can pass on promoter votes while most institutions vote against
The Tata 2016 and ICICI Bank 2018 episodes show both risks: independent directors removed for dissenting, and boards defending management before investigating
